title: Hydrogen-induced Fractures in Large Fasteners
abstract: Abstract Wind power plants and heavy steel construction require the use of large-scale bolts of property class 10.9. Due to their high strength, however, these fasteners are subject to an increased susceptibility to hydrogen-induced stress corrosion cracking (SCC). Under tensile stress, this degradation mechanism leads to brittle, time-delayed failure—without any prior visible warning. This poses a severe risk to structural integrity and, in the event of failure, incurs significant costs due to unplanned downtime and extensive repair efforts. This contribution presents selected failure cases involving large-scale bolts with dimensions ranging from M42 to M64, which fractured within a few weeks or months after installation as a result of hydrogen-induced stress corrosion cracking. The root causes of failure can be categorized into susceptible material conditions, coating-related factors, and installation-related factors. In manufacturing, impermissible surface carburization—which leads to hardness values significantly exceeding the permitted limit—as well as defects in the hot-dip galvanizing process pose a substantial risk. An often-underestimated influencing factor is the installation practice. Weather-related impacts on the thread surfaces drastically alter the coefficients of friction. In torque-controlled tightening procedures, this can result in uncontrolled preload forces that exceed the design criteria. Selected failure cases are presented based on fractographic, microanalytical, and microstructural investigations. Furthermore, the presentation highlights the degradation process underlying hydrogen-induced stress corrosion cracking, the normative framework, and the correlation between material susceptibility and hydrogen content.

sections.heading: Introduction and Research Context
paragraphs: The reliable transmission of large loads in modern plant engineering, particularly in wind turbines and heavy structural steelwork, increasingly requires the use of high strength, large-format bolts of property class 10.9. However, with increasing performance demands and growing structural dimensions, the materials-related challenges for these fasteners, which contribute significantly to structural integrity and operational safety, are also rising. At the same time, the risk of damage due to hydrogen-induced stress corrosion cracking (H-SCC) increases. This failure mechanism is particularly critical because, under mechanical tensile stress, it leads to a brittle, delayed failure—completely without prior warning [ 1 ,  2 – 3 ]. For affected structures, this represents a massive safety risk that causes significant economic costs in the event of failure due to unplanned downtimes and high repair efforts.

H‑SCC occurs due to the interaction of three main factors: a susceptible material condition, a critical hydrogen availability, and mechanical tensile stresses (Fig.  1 ; [ 2 ,  4 ]). Fig. 1 Hydrogen induced stress corrosion cracking and factors of influence [ 2 ]

The failure process takes place in three consecutive phases: production- or environment-induced hydrogen absorption at the component surface, subsequent diffusion of hydrogen within the metal lattice to areas of maximum stress triaxiality or maximum lattice expansion, and finally, crack initiation (Fig.  2 ). To explain the atomic processes at the crack tip, two main established models exist: the HEDE (Hydrogen-enhanced Decohesion) model postulates a hydrogen-induced reduction of atomic cohesive forces at the grain boundaries [ 5 ,  6 ], whereas the HELP (Hydrogen-enhanced Local Plasticity) model assumes a locally facilitated dislocation movement and associated localized plasticization [ 7 ,  8 ]. Fig. 2 Cause of failure for hydrogen induced stress corrosion cracking

Although the hydrogen susceptibility of high-strength steels is linked to their strength and guidelines often indicate a hazard starting from a tensile strength of 1000 MPa, strength alone is not the decisive factor. Through optimizations in chemical composition and microstructure, susceptibility can be significantly reduced [ 9 ,  10 ]; conversely, failures are also possible below 1000 MPa if an unfavorable material condition is present.

These materials-related relationships are only incompletely covered by current regulatory frameworks. DIN EN ISO 898‑1, the fundamental standard for steel bolts, contains warnings regarding stress corrosion cracking only from property class 12.9 onwards and requires the avoidance of phosphorus-induced delta ferrite, which weakens the grain boundaries. For bolts of property class 10.9, corresponding warnings are entirely missing from this basic standard. Although DIN EN 14399‑4 notes for class 10.9 HV bolts that the risk of hydrogen embrittlement must be taken into account through a suitable surface treatment, the DASt Guideline 021, which applies to large fasteners from M39 onwards, does not address the topic. A significant advancement is provided by the guideline of the German Fastener Association (Deutscher Schraubenverband e. V.—DSV) and the Joint Galvanizing Committee (Gemeinschaftsausschuss Verzinken e. V.—GAV), published back in 2009. This guideline prohibits the occurrence of delta ferrite starting from property class 10.9, tightens the limit values for phosphorus and sulfur, limits the maximum tensile strength to a maximum of 1170 N/mm 2  or the surface hardness to a maximum of 375 HV 0.3, and tightens the requirements for permissible surface defects in accordance with DIN EN 26157‑3.

Nevertheless, brittle fractures continue to occur in practice, particularly in large-format bolts with dimensions ranging from M42 to M64. The focus of this work is the systematic materials science investigation of failures in HV bolts of sizes M42 to M64. Based on fractographic, microanalytical (EDX), and microstructural examinations of metallographic sections, the complex interaction of unfavorable material conditions, manufacturing-induced pre-damage (such as LMAC), and real assembly influences is analyzed. The objective is to raise awareness of these critical failure mechanisms in components of property class 10.9 and to contribute practical insights for preventing future failures.

sections.heading: Initial Situation
paragraphs: Some time after assembly, delayed fractures occurred in several hot-dip galvanized high-strength (HV) bolting assemblies of dimension M42 × 280 (property class 10.9) in an onshore wind farm. Preloading of the visually inconspicuous connections was torque-controlled using hydraulic torque wrenches. According to the corresponding inspection certificate, a mean k‑factor (total coefficient of friction) of 0.130 was reported for the batch. The bolts were assembled using the mounting torque specified by the DASt Guideline 021 for HV bolts of size M42, which was T m  = 4500 Nm. To systematically adjust and stabilize this coefficient of friction, the nuts were factory-provided with a solid lubricant based on MoS 2  with PTFE additives.

Since the raw material used for bolt manufacturing was processed in a non-phosphated state, an embrittling delta ferrite formation due to insufficient dephosphatization during heat treatment can be excluded on the process side. Furthermore, the component surfaces were mechanically cleaned by blasting prior to hot-dip galvanizing; a production-related hydrogen absorption via pickling processes can therefore also be ruled out. During the actual tightening process as well as immediately after assembly, no recognizable anomalies or irregularities were documented that could primarily be linked directly to the subsequent cause of fracture.

sections.heading: Investigation Results
paragraphs: The fractures of the investigated M42 bolts occurred in the area of the first load-bearing thread turn (Fig.  3 a). During the dismantling and accompanying inspection of undamaged reference bolts from the affected wind farm, macroscopically visible plastic elongation (stretching) could be detected on several components (Fig.  3 b). Distinctly recognizable whitish deposits were visible both in the transition radius from the shank to the bolt head and on the hot-dip galvanized thread surfaces (Fig.  3 c, d). These were macroscopically identified as white rust—a typical corrosion product of the zinc coating—and provide a clear indication of an operationally induced hydrogen supply resulting from cathodic corrosion reactions. The investigation of these deposits carried out by means of energy-dispersive X‑ray microanalysis (EDX) (Fig.  3 e) detected a significant chlorine signal in addition to zinc oxide, confirming the damaging influence of a chloride-containing, corrosive medium. Fig. 3 a  Broken M42 × 280 bolt assembly from an onshore wind turbine,  b  disassembled and elongated bolt from the same structure,  c  and  d  fracture area from  a  showing localized whitish deposits in the thread,  e  exemplary EDX analysis of the whitish deposit,  f  microcrack in the thread root of the broken bolt after stripping the zinc coating

Due to the detected plastic deformation of the dismantled bolts, the zinc coatings in the fracture and thread regions were chemically stripped in inhibited hydrochloric acid to analyze the underlying base material via scanning electron microscopy (SEM). After removing the zinc layer, all fractured specimens exhibited fine, transverse microcracks in the thread roots of the freely loaded thread section (Fig.  3 f). In contrast, intact reference bolts without signs of macroscopic elongation did not show any crack-like damage in the thread root.

The fracture surfaces of the damaged components macroscopically exhibited a characteristic, nearly concentric rim with a flat fracture topography as well as fracture propagation paths running radially toward the center (Fig.  4 a). Toward the center of the fracture surface, fractography revealed an increasingly rugged and more pronounced topography. Within the flat concentric rim, an intergranular cleavage fracture with quasi-cleavage components was present (Fig.  4 b, c). These quasi-cleavage structures continuously increased with ongoing fracture propagation toward the center of the specimen, with initial ductile components appearing at the boundary of the rim. The center of the fracture surface was completely characterized by dimple structures corresponding to a transgranular dimple fracture (Fig.  4 d). Overall, the fractographic findings are characteristic of hydrogen-induced stress corrosion cracking (H-SCC). Fig. 4 a  Exemplary fracture surface of a broken M24 × 280 bolt,  b ,  c  exemplary micrographs of the fracture microstructure in the region of the flat concentric rim: intergranular cleavage fracture with quasi-cleavage fractions,  d  fracture microstructure in the center of the fracture surface: transgranular ductile fracture

To ensure microstructural verification, metallographic longitudinal sections were prepared through the freely loaded thread sections of three representative states: a dismantled, non-elongated bolt, a fractured bolt, and a dismantled, elongated bolt. While the thread root and the layer morphology of the zinc coating showed an inconspicuous finding for the non-elongated reference bolt (Fig.  5 a), the section images of the fractured bolt revealed gaping separations within the zinc coating that continued as sharp microcracks into the steel base material (Fig.  5 b). An analogous damage pattern with deep, gaping cracks in the thread root was observed in the dismantled but plastically deformed bolt (Fig.  5 c). Fig. 5 a  Thread root of a non-elongated bolt,  b  thread root of the broken bolt from Fig.  3 a with gaping separations in the zinc coating extending as cracks into the base material,  c  thread root of the elongated bolt from Fig.  3 b with flaking of the zinc coating and distinct, gaping microcracks in the base material

The hardness measurements carried out on the section specimens in the core material yielded homogeneous and inconspicuous values between (342 ± 11 HV 10) and (351 ± 12) HV 10. Thus, the strength properties are within the permissible range of (320–380) HV 10 for property class 10.9 according to DIN EN ISO 898‑1. The verification of the decarburization/carburization state according to the specifications of DIN EN ISO 898‑1 was also negative; there were no indications of impermissible surface decarburization or carburization.

sections.heading: Conclusion
paragraphs: The results of the metallographic and fractographic investigations prove that the bolting assemblies were already locally stressed into the plastic range during the assembly process. Taking into account the friction coefficient of k = 0.13 reported in the inspection certificate, a calculated tensile stress of around 736 MPa results in the bolt shank under the applied mounting torque. Relative to the nominal yield strength of property class 10.9 of 940 MPa and the planned utilization of 70%, this mechanical stress lies approximately 13% above the theoretical target value of 658 MPa. In relation to the actual yield strength of the delivered batch of 1021 MPa, however, the applied preload correlates very well with the target value of 70% of the actual yield strength.

As part of the root cause analysis, indications intensified that the assembly of several bolted connections significantly deviated from the applicable specifications. Accordingly, the bolt studs and nuts were exposed unprotected to the wet weather conditions for several days before final tightening. The direct contact with moisture and the formation of white rust on the hot-dip galvanized surfaces led to an uncontrolled alteration of the friction coefficients.

Since the induced preload force in a torque-controlled tightening process highly depends on the friction coefficient, an environmentally reduced friction under constant tightening torque causes an unintentionally increased axial preload force. In the present case, a reduction of the friction coefficient to k < 0.1 would already cause the actual yield strength of the bolt to be exceeded under otherwise identical assembly conditions.

The cracks generated in the thread root as a result of this over-elastic assembly cause an additional local notch effect. Simultaneously, they form entry paths for corrosion-induced hydrogen, which can be absorbed by the material at these locations. This interaction ultimately triggered the delayed failure due to hydrogen-induced stress corrosion cracking (H-SCC).

sections.heading: Initial Situation
paragraphs: The second failure case involves delayed fractures of large-format hexagon bolts of dimension M64 × 530 of property class 10.9, which were used for the assembly of onshore tower flange connections in wind turbines. For corrosion protection, a zinc flake coating was applied. Aggressive environmental influences at the installation site—such as a pronounced proximity to the coast, industrial atmosphere or agricultural emissions—could be ruled out.

Approximately three to four weeks after installation, bolt fractures were detected, even though the connections had been exposed to no dynamic operating loads up to that point, but exclusively to the static preload force. The fractures occurred in the transition radius from the bolt head to the shank. Faulty assembly or exceeding the tightening torque was ruled out; the planned elastic utilization of the bolts was approximately 84% of the component-specific yield strength.

The accompanying inspection certificate from the East Asian manufacturer certified the conformity of the mechanical properties with the requirements of DIN EN ISO 898‑1 for property class 10.9. A carburization test using a three-point hardness measurement listed in the certificate also showed ostensibly inconspicuous characteristic values. However, this introduces a fundamental materials-related contradiction to the manufacturing specification that the threads were final thread rolled after heat treatment: due to the associated work hardening in the thread root, a normative carburization test via the three-point hardness method according to DIN EN ISO 898‑1 is methodologically impossible. The deformation-induced microstructural hardening inevitably leads to an increase in hardness in the thread root, which impermissibly overlays the material-dependent measurement values of a potential carburization and makes a correct differentiation impossible.

sections.heading: Investigation Results
paragraphs: Figure  6 a exemplarily shows the macroscopic appearance of a fractured M64 bolt. From a macroscopic perspective, the fracture occurred completely without deformation in the transition region between the head bearing surface and the shank. Apart from secondary flash rust formation on the fracture surfaces, no corrosion products were visible macroscopically on the zinc flake-coated surfaces. The macroscopic fracture surface examination provides indications of multiple fracture origins characterized by fine steps, extending along the circumference between the 2 o’clock and the 12 o’clock positions (Fig.  6 b). In this crack initiation zone—apart from varying fracture planes—a distinctly flat topography is present. Starting from the center of the fracture surface and moving toward the 1 o’clock circumferential position, a rugged topography is visible, which characterizes the final crack propagation area. Fig. 6 a  Broken M64 × 530 bolt from an onshore wind turbine,  b  shaft-side fracture surface with secondary flash rust,  c  exemplary micrograph of the fracture microstructure near a fracture origin: intergranular cleavage fracture with quasi-cleavage fractions,  d  increasing quasi-cleavage fractions during further crack propagation,  e  transgranular ductile fracture at the final fracture zone

The microfractographic analysis of the fracture microstructure using SEM reveals a failure pattern that is completely characteristic of hydrogen-induced stress corrosion cracking (H-SCC): a brittle, intergranular cleavage fracture with quasi-cleavage components dominates the immediate boundary region (Fig.  6 c). With ongoing fracture propagation, the intergranular fraction continuously decreases, while the quasi-cleavage fracture structures increase (Fig.  6 d). Finally, the remaining fracture zone is characterized by a distinctive dimpled ductile shear fracture (Fig.  6 e).
For microstructural characterization, metallographic longitudinal microsections were prepared from the head-to-shank radius as well as along the thread profile.

Isolated surface imperfections in the form of overlaps are present in the boundary zone, particularly near the head-to-shank transition radius (Fig.  7 a, b). Both near the fracture and along the thread profile, a darkly etched seam is visible after contrasting, which exhibits the classic microstructural characteristics of pronounced surface carburization (Fig.  7 c to f). A misinterpretation as a purely preparation-induced etching artifact, which can typically occur due to the electrochemical protective effect of zinc coatings in metallographic sections, was reliably ruled out. Fig. 7 a ,  b  Surface imperfections near the transition between the head bearing surface and the shank,  c  etched overview micrograph of the fracture zone showing a dark carburized layer,  d  detailed view of the carburized layer,  e  etched overview micrograph of the thread showing pronounced carburization at the thread tip  f  detailed view of a thread root with a carburized layer as well as elongation of the microstructure due to final thread rolling

The effective depth of this carburized surface layer is approximately 200 µm along the shank section. Within the thread turns, the carburization zone appears characteristically irregular as a result of the plastic material deformation caused by the final thread rolling process: while the carburization seam is clearly distinguishable at the less deformed thread tip, it appears optically less sharply defined in the thread root due to the material deformation. In the thread root, the elongation of the microstructure due to the final rolling process is clearly pronounced. With the exception of this carburization seam, the core microstructure presents itself as a typical tempered martensite.

Taking into account the deformation-induced work hardening from final thread rolling as well as the verified carburization, the values of the three-point hardness test specified in the inspection certificate are implausible. For the standard-compliant determination of the surface hardness according to DIN EN ISO 898‑1, the zinc flake coating was gently removed mechanically, after which hardness measurements were carried out both on the shank and on the widths across flats of the bolt heads. The determined measurement values between (444 ± 33) HV 0.3 and (485 ± 34) HV 0.3 correlate well with the carburized boundary zone observed in the microsections. At the same time, the maximum upper limit for surface hardness specified in DIN EN ISO 898‑1 for property class 10.9 bolts of max. 390 HV 0.3 is significantly exceeded. Conversely, the core hardness values ranging from (354 ± 12) HV 10 to (361 ± 12 HV 10) are completely inconspicuous and comply with the normative requirements for property class 10.9 bolts.

sections.heading: Conclusion
paragraphs: Both the delayed failure sequence and the fractographic SEM findings clearly indicate hydrogen-induced stress corrosion cracking (H-SCC) as the primary cause of fracture. A production-related hydrogen absorption can be ruled out on the process side, as the component surfaces were cleaned exclusively mechanically by blasting prior to the application of the zinc flake coating. Although, in contrast to the previous failure case, no macroscopically conspicuous corrosion products were detected in the threads, an operationally induced hydrogen entry is highly plausible. Weather-related moisture during the erection phase as well as condensate formation due to repeated falling below the dew point lead to an inconspicuous but continuous surface reaction: here, the zinc content of the coating reacts with the moisture, whereby diffusible, atomic hydrogen is released and can be absorbed by the material.

The pronounced surface carburization represents an impermissible deviation from the requirements of DIN EN ISO 898‑1. With measured surface hardness values of up to 485 HV 0.3, the normative limit of a maximum of 390 HV 0.3 is massively exceeded, which leads to an embrittlement of the surface zone and increased susceptibility to H‑SCC. The surface imperfections detected in the transition radius in the form of overlaps also act as geometric notches that induce local stress concentrations and increase the risk of crack formation.

In the course of further research, it turned out that the East Asian manufacturer used an in-house, non-standardized test method to evaluate the carburization, in which measurement points of a longitudinal section through the thread were combined with those of a cross-section through the shank. This methodologically flawed practice, which was not declared in the inspection certificate, provided misleadingly inconspicuous test values that were falsely attributed to the standard-compliant methodology according to DIN EN ISO 898‑1. The subsequent argumentation of the manufacturer that surface carburization is unavoidable due to the process for such large dimensions and that the validity of DIN EN ISO 898‑1 only includes dimensions up to M39 is completely groundless from a materials engineering perspective.

Instead, the long-standing experience of the MPA Darmstadt proves that high-strength bolts of dimension M64 and larger can easily be manufactured without carburization and in a sufficiently tough material condition. In industrial practice, the mechanical and metallurgical properties defined in DIN EN ISO 898‑1 are by default adopted as dimensions > M39. In further regulations such as the DSV-GAV guideline or the DASt Guideline 021, these requirements for large components are sometimes even provided with even more restrictive limitations, e.g., regarding the maximum surface hardness, in order to reduce the hydrogen embrittlement susceptibility.

sections.heading: Summary
paragraphs: The failure cases presented illustrate that, in order to prevent hydrogen-induced damage, consistent compliance with manufacturer-side product requirements from standards and regulations is indispensable. Corresponding specifications, such as installation guidelines, must also be strictly observed on the user side to ensure the structural integrity of modern large-scale plants.

For the investigation and prevention of failures, independent failure analysis by competent testing laboratories is of particular importance, as the interactions between material selection, component manufacturing, corrosion protection, and assembly are highly complex. Frequently, an interplay of multiple factors comes into effect, promoting the occurrence of damage.
